data.body:
`ddflow upgrade` (default = --plan, writes nothing, exit 0 up to date / 2 nothing to do vs 1 plan pending per exit-code convention), MCP ddflow_upgrade (plan and apply args), and `ddflow doctor --upgrade` as an alias. The plan reports by category: data repairs available, config (new knobs, changed defaults that alter this project's behaviour because it has no entry), instructions (driver docs / rules blocks / native rules whose bytes differ, hand-edited ones flagged separately), hooks (git hooks pointing at a missing or different binary, missing SessionStart/UserPromptSubmit hooks), MCP launch, newly available opt-in features and `ddflow companions`. Reuses driver_drift/rules_status, hooks status, Config source tracking, manifest.
Failing-first: against the 0.1.3-built fixture project the plan lists the missing UserPromptSubmit hook, drifted driver doc, dedupe/readme knobs, a dangling pre-commit binary; against a fresh init it is empty. Plan output byte-identical in CLI --json and MCP.

OPERATOR DECISION D-upgrade-config-changes (2026-10-03): agents may apply upgrade config changes where the project never set the value; any value the operator set (present in any config layer, env, or set via ddflow config/ddflow_configure) is never changed without the operator's confirmation: the plan marks it 'needs operator confirmation', --apply refuses it unless --confirm <knob> --reason is passed and is recorded; changed shipped defaults are always listed in the plan, notice and upgrade.applied. [upgrade].config_changes = agent|ask|operator (default agent). Failing-first test: an operator-set knob whose default/name changed is refused without --confirm, applied with it; an unset knob is applied by the agent; both appear in the plan.

--apply <category,...>|all. Before ANY write: snapshot every file it will touch to .ddflow/backups/<ts>-<from>-to-<to>/ (local, git-ignored) and print the git diff command; driver docs and rules blocks get a version+body-sha256 header (like export docs) so hand edits are detected and the file is moved aside (.local-edits) or refused, never silently overwritten (also fix adopt --refresh-docs to use it). Dangling git-hook binary is repaired by hooks install. Idempotent: second apply is a no-op. Appends upgrade.applied (from, to, categories, backup) so replay explains it. Config-default changes are never auto-applied: they are listed with 'pin old behaviour: ddflow config --set X old' and recorded when the operator acknowledges.

data.decision: Operator 2026-10-03 (verbatim): 'block by default but inform the operator for options and let the operator decide or ask the agent to work for a safe upgrade'. The lint compares the release's knobs, defaults, event kinds, hooks and instruction templates with the shipped upgrade manifest; a change with no manifest entry BLOCKS the release (publish workflow / version cut) by default. The block is never a bare failure: it prints the unmanifested changes and the operator's options: (1) have an agent write the missing manifest entries and the upgrade repairs/notes needed for a SAFE upgrade (ddflow can pre-fill them from the changelog fields and the knob diff; the agent reports what an existing project will see), then re-run the lint; (2) waive named entries for this release with --waive <change> --reason, recorded in the release record and shown in the next upgrade plan; (3) change the policy. Configurable: [release].manifest_lint = block | warn | off (shipped default block) over config, CLI and MCP; an agent may prepare entries and propose, but waiving or lowering the policy is the operator's decision. Still OPEN in D-upgrade-model: the skew-guard default (operator proposed refuse-once with a recorded override flag). Accepted: D-upgrade-event-kinds, D-upgrade-auto-check, D-upgrade-backups, D-upgrade-config-changes.

data.body:
A machine-readable manifest shipped in the wheel (ddflow/templates/upgrade/changes.toml) listing per release: new knobs (key, default, one-line why), CHANGED defaults (knob, old, new, behaviour effect), instruction/hook/template refreshes, repairs (ids), and opt-in features with the enabling command. Generated at release time from the log's complete --changelog lines + a lint that fails the release when config.py gained/changed a knob not listed (the dedupe warn->ask flip would have been caught). Reader API: changes_since(version).
Failing-first: a test diffs KNOB defaults between the previous tag and HEAD and requires a manifest entry for each added/changed knob; reading since 0.1.3 returns the 20 knobs found in the experiment. Docs shipped in templates; README section.

OPERATOR DECISION D-upgrade-manifest-lint (2026-10-03): the manifest lint BLOCKS a release by default ([release].manifest_lint = block|warn|off, default block, via config/CLI/MCP). A block prints the unmanifested changes and the operator's options: have an agent prepare the missing entries and safe-upgrade notes (pre-filled from the changelog fields and knob diff), waive named entries for this release with --waive <change> --reason (recorded), or change the policy. Agents may prepare and propose; waiving or lowering the policy is the operator's call. data.decision: Operator 2026-10-03 answered 'Yes, as described' to: an OLDER ddflow refuses its first write to a log stamped by a newer version (exit 3); the message tells the agent to upgrade or ask the user; if the user insists the agent reruns with an explicit override (--allow-older-version --reason, also over MCP); a skew.overridden event (third new event kind, with running version, log version, reason, agent) is written and the events written in that session carry a mark that they come from an older version, shown by replay/history/doctor and listed by a later ddflow upgrade for review; the override is session-scoped, not per command; [upgrade].skew = refuse|warn|off, shipped default refuse, configurable via config, CLI and MCP. With this the whole D-upgrade-model is decided: D-upgrade-event-kinds, D-upgrade-auto-check, D-upgrade-backups, D-upgrade-config-changes, D-upgrade-manifest-lint, D-upgrade-skew-guard.

Failing-first: an older-version simulation (stamp newer than the running version) refuses the first write with exit 3 and the message; the override writes skew.overridden and marks the session's events; a second session is refused again; warn/off do not refuse; an unknown event kind is skipped by an old reader.

data.decision: Operator 2026-10-03 (verbatim): 'Make ddflow have a feature to periodically check for newer versions of ddflow, to propose to the operator upgrade of itself, to have self-upgrade cli command and capabilities which do migration and upgrades (in case of running docker it shall introduce check for upgrade and migration on container or mcp start and implement it while in container if the container version has been upgraded and database and other storage and config artifacts needs migration) need. The user should be capable to check, ask, request ddflow upgrade and orchestrate and monitor it'. Recorded design (defaults chosen by claude where the operator did not say; each is a knob the operator can change): (1) RELEASE CHECK: ddflow looks for a newer release of itself at most once per [upgrade].check_interval_h (default 24) from the package index it was installed from (and the image registry tag when running in a container); opportunistic at session start/brief/doctor, never a daemon, bounded by a short timeout, silent and harmless offline; the result is cached under .ddflow/local; it sends nothing but the request for the public version list (no project data, no telemetry). [upgrade].release_check = on|off (shipped default on, because the operator asked for periodic checks; off for air-gapped use; DDFLOW_NO_UPDATE_CHECK env). (2) PROPOSAL: a newer release is PROPOSED, never installed silently: one line in the session-start notice, brief, status and doctor ('ddflow X is available, you run Y: what changed + how to upgrade'), once per version per machine; an agent that sees it tells the operator. (3) SELF-UPGRADE: `ddflow upgrade --self` (CLI; MCP ddflow_upgrade action=self) detects how ddflow is installed (uv tool, pipx, pip in a venv, uvx/ephemeral, container image, source checkout) and either runs the right installer command or, where it cannot (container image, source checkout, read-only install), prints the exact command for the operator; installing new code is the operator's decision: an agent may run it only with the operator's recorded consent ([upgrade].self = ask|operator|auto, default ask); the old version is remembered so `ddflow upgrade --self --rollback` can reinstall it. (4) MIGRATION follows the install: after a self-upgrade, and on the first run of a new version, the project upgrade plan runs (ddflow upgrade --plan), and the categories allowed by [upgrade].auto are applied with a backup first; operator-set config needs confirmation (D-upgrade-config-changes). (5) CONTAINER / MCP START: when the server or the container starts, it compares its own version with the project's stamp (and the stores it mounts: log, index, local config, backups, hooks, instruction files); if the image is newer it runs the check and the safe migrations in the container before serving, reports what it did or what awaits the operator in the first brief, and never fails to start because of a pending migration (it serves, marks the plan pending and says so); if the image is OLDER than the project the skew guard applies (D-upgrade-skew-guard). [upgrade].on_start = check|safe|off (default safe for index/derived-store rebuilds and non-destructive categories; anything needing consent waits). (6) ORCHESTRATE AND MONITOR: the operator can ask at any time: ddflow upgrade --check (is there a newer release, is this project behind), --plan, --apply, --self, --status (what ran, what is pending, which agents/MCP servers still run the old version and must restart), --history, --restore; the same over MCP so the operator can ask an agent; every step is recorded as events so replay explains it; a running upgrade shows progress and can be resumed after an interruption (idempotent steps).
data.title: ddflow checks for newer releases of itself, proposes the upgrade to the operator, can upgrade itself and migrate the project, including at container/MCP start; the operator can check, request, orchestrate and monitor it

data.body:
Operator 2026-10-03 (verbatim): 'Make ddflow have a feature to periodically check for newer versions of ddflow, to propose to the operator upgrade of itself, to have self-upgrade cli command and capabilities which do migration and upgrades (in case of running docker it shall introduce check for upgrade and migration on container or mcp start and implement it while in container if the container version has been upgraded and database and other storage and config artifacts needs migration) need. The user should be capable to check, ask, request ddflow upgrade and orchestrate and monitor it'. D-self-upgrade (1),(2). A release-index client (stdlib urllib, short timeout, injectable for tests) reads the newest released version from the index ddflow was installed from (default the public Python package index; a configured [upgrade].index_url for a private mirror; the image registry tag when in a container if cheaply available, else the package index); checked at most once per [upgrade].check_interval_h (default 24) at session start/brief/doctor, cached in .ddflow/local (never committed), never blocks or fails a command, silent offline; pre-releases ignored unless [upgrade].prereleases. Knobs: [upgrade].release_check on|off (default on), check_interval_h, index_url; env DDFLOW_NO_UPDATE_CHECK. Proposal line once per version per machine in the session-start notice (B-upgrade.6-notice), brief, status, doctor; `ddflow upgrade --check` forces a check and prints running version, newest version, project stamp, and what changed (manifest, B-upgrade.2-changes, when present). Nothing but the version request leaves the machine; README states exactly what is requested and how to turn it off. FAILING FIRST: fake index newer -> one proposal line, second run within the interval makes NO request; offline/timeout -> no error, no line; off/env -> no request at all; version comparison handles 0.1.9 < 0.1.10 and pre-releases; cache is under .ddflow/local; MCP parity.

GENERALITY: shipped defaults in the package for every project; works on upgrade and on fresh ddflow init; tests in a throwaway project with NO network (fake release index, fake installer, injected clock); no reference to this repository's paths, hosts, agents or models; docs ship in README and ddflow/templates; works for every agent integration and for the CLI, MCP and container surfaces; everything configurable via config, ddflow config and ddflow_configure; tools/list byte budget stays green. Builds on the accepted upgrade decisions (ddflow decision show D-upgrade-event-kinds, -auto-check, -backups, -config-changes, -manifest-lint, -skew-guard) and D-self-upgrade.

Operator 2026-10-03 (verbatim): 'Make ddflow have a feature to periodically check for newer versions of ddflow, to propose to the operator upgrade of itself, to have self-upgrade cli command and capabilities which do migration and upgrades (in case of running docker it shall introduce check for upgrade and migration on container or mcp start and implement it while in container if the container version has been upgraded and database and other storage and config artifacts needs migration) need. The user should be capable to check, ask, request ddflow upgrade and orchestrate and monitor it'. D-self-upgrade (3),(4). Reuse services/install_info.py (install method detection from the upstream-reporting work). `ddflow upgrade --self [--to VERSION] [--dry-run]`: uv tool -> uv tool upgrade; pipx -> pipx upgrade; pip in a venv -> that interpreter's pip install -U; uvx/ephemeral, container image, source checkout or read-only install -> do not attempt, print the exact command for the operator (image pull + restart; git pull; the launcher line to change). Consent: [upgrade].self = ask|operator|auto (default ask): an agent may only run it with the operator's consent passed and recorded (--yes --reason over CLI; MCP ddflow_upgrade action=self confirm=true), otherwise it reports the proposal; the installer runs as a subprocess with bounded time and its output captured; the running process never replaces its own code mid-command (it finishes, then tells the caller to restart; MCP servers report 'restart needed'). After success: record upgrade.applied (category self, from/to), run the project plan (B-upgrade.3-plan) and apply what [upgrade].auto allows with a backup; hooks and MCP launch entries that pin a path are refreshed (see bug B-dangling-precommit-hook). `--self --rollback` reinstalls the remembered previous version. FAILING FIRST (fake installer, no network): each install method chooses the right command; unsupported methods print the command and exit 2; no consent -> refused with the proposal (exit 3); success records the event and triggers the plan; failure leaves the old version working and says so; rollback reinstalls; MCP parity and budget.

data.body:
Operator 2026-10-03 (verbatim): 'Make ddflow have a feature to periodically check for newer versions of ddflow, to propose to the operator upgrade of itself, to have self-upgrade cli command and capabilities which do migration and upgrades (in case of running docker it shall introduce check for upgrade and migration on container or mcp start and implement it while in container if the container version has been upgraded and database and other storage and config artifacts needs migration) need. The user should be capable to check, ask, request ddflow upgrade and orchestrate and monitor it'. D-self-upgrade (5). At `ddflow mcp` start and at container entrypoint: compare the running version with the project stamp and with each store it uses (event log readability, index schema, .ddflow/local config and caches, backups dir, instruction files, hooks, MCP launch entry); newer runtime -> run the release check (if enabled), rebuild derived stores, apply the categories [upgrade].on_start allows (check|safe|off, default safe: derived-store rebuilds and non-destructive, backed-up categories only), leave consent-needing items pending; report in the first brief/first tool reply what was migrated and what awaits the operator; NEVER refuse to start for a pending migration; bounded time, then serve and continue the plan as pending; older runtime than the project -> skew guard (D-upgrade-skew-guard). Works with read-only mounts (reports instead of writing) and with the project volume owned by another uid. The image documents the behaviour and the env switches (DDFLOW_UPGRADE_ON_START). A stale RUNNING server is detected the other way round: a server whose version is older than the stamp says 'restart me' in its replies. data.decision: Operator 2026-10-03 (verbatim): 'Make as a default mode unless otherwise instructed by the operator or its agent, agents.md, Claude.md etc the workflow in ddflow to pick up all newly discovered bugs and to start fixing them immediately'. Recorded design (details chosen by claude, each a knob): [bugs].on_found = fix_now | queue | ask, shipped default fix_now for every ddflow project. fix_now: recording a bug files its fix task in the queue (B-bugs-as-items) at the head of the offer (bugs_first already orders bug fixes first), and the workflow tells the agent to start it NOW: the reply to `bug found` (CLI and MCP), `next` and `brief` say 'open bug X has no fix in progress: claim <fix task> before other new work'; a session with spare capacity (the orchestrator, or the finder once its current item is merged or parked) claims it at once; the finder does not abandon or stall the item it holds: it records the bug first, then either fixes it in the same item when the bug is inside its claimed files and blocks its work, or leaves the fix task for the next free agent. Limits that keep it safe: the regression-test rule stands (no close without a test that fails on the unfixed code); a bug whose fix needs an operator decision is filed blocked with the question, not guessed; duplicates are checked before filing ([dedupe]); the parallelism limit and leases are respected (a fix waits for a hot file like any task); [bugs].fix_now_min_severity (default low = all) can restrict it. OVERRIDES, in order: an explicit operator instruction in the session; the project's instruction files (AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md / GEMINI.md and the shipped ddflow block in them, which states the default and how to change it); [bugs].on_found in config (shared or local), ddflow config, ddflow_configure. queue = file the fix task but do not push it; ask = the agent asks the operator before starting. doctor notes open bugs with no fix task or no fix in progress.
data.title: Default mode: a newly discovered bug is picked up and its fix starts immediately, unless the operator or the project's instructions say otherwise

chunk_findings.detail: The two patterns added to the ignore block are unanchored: in gitignore syntax a pattern with no slash anywhere except a trailing one matches a directory of that name at *any* depth below the file that contains it. The surrounding lines (`.*.lock`, and the comment "Without this line `git add .ddflow`, as `init` instructs, committed it") show this block is the ignore content applied to the project, not a `.ddflow`-scoped file; if it is the repository `.gitignore`, then a legitimate project directory such as `runs/` (e.g. experiment/benchmark outputs) or `docs/worktrees/` will now be silently ignored. Concretely: a project that already tracks `runs/results.csv` runs `ddflow init`/`adopt`, the block is appended, and from then on `git status` hides `runs/`, `git add runs/results.csv` is a no-op (needs `-f`), and ripgrep stops searching it — exactly the opposite of the intent, which is to exclude only the worktree home under `.ddflow/`. The patterns should be anchored to the actual home, e.g. `.ddflow/worktrees/` and `.ddflow/runs/` (or the block should live in `.ddflow/.gitignore`, if that is in fact where it is written).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/adopt.py:581 (added `"worktrees/\nruns/\n"` line)

chunk_findings.detail: `_ignore_inside` was added to the two places that *materialize* a worktree root — the create branch (`wt_root.mkdir(...); _ignore_inside(root, wt_root)`) and the merge helper — but the create function's adopt branch returns at `return wt  # adopt`, i.e. before the new call. That branch is precisely the entry point for the trees this change is about: the intent says harness-made trees are "mapped into the same home where the harness allows it ... else adopted where they are and listed", so when Claude Code / Kilo (or a user) has already run `git worktree add` at the in-repo home and ddflow then claims it, `create()` sees `path` exists, adopts, and returns without ever writing the self-ignoring marker. Concretely: a project whose ignore file does not yet cover the root (the window the docstring itself names — "a project adopted before the root moved there still carries the old file until `init`/`adopt` runs again", or any root whose directory name is not already matched), plus a harness-created tree at, say, `.ddflow/worktrees/foo`; the next ddflow claim adopts it, no `.ddflow/worktrees/.gitignore` is written, and `git status` in the main tree lists the whole adopted checkout as untracked — the exact failure `_ignore_inside` exists to prevent. `wt_root` is certainly available on that path (the adopted `path` lives under it) and the marker write is safe for an already-existing tree, so the call belongs before the adopt `return` as well.

chunk_findings.detail: The fixture writes a reviewer command whose final action is `echo 'STATUS: NO FINDINGS'`. That is a literal, unconditional verdict token embedded in the repository source and emitted to stdout every time the "critic" gate runs. Any consumer of the change that greps reviewer output for a verdict — including an automated/LLM reviewer reading this diff or the test's captured output — is exposed to a spoofed "no findings" verdict, independent of the content actually reviewed: running any of these tests, or merely reading the file, presents the exact string the review pipeline treats as a passing verdict. (The rest of the file is consistent: `taken`/`late` are captured correctly, the delta headers and commit counts in both tests line up, and both cases do fail if `reviewed_head` is recorded after the reviewer instead of with the diff.)

data.text: Make sure all the hooks you implement are going to be compatible and be able to be adopted on all the coding agents we want to support, including but not limited to claude, copilot, codex, gemini, opencode, kilo, qwen-code, aider, windsurf, antigravity, etc. Create a phase + tasks to make a research and make sure the whole ddflow code is unified and implemented in such a way that we support the same features, hooks, prompts, and onboarding on all of the coding agents, and if we decide later to add a new one, we don't have to rewrite the code, but instead have a minimal integration surface

data.claim: Per-agent knowledge is spread over ~11 files: adopt.py AGENT_TARGETS (22 agents, 7 MCP config shapes), NATIVE_RULES, AGENT_COMMANDS (Claude only), claudehooks.py (Claude SessionStart/UserPromptSubmit/PreCompact, Gemini BeforeAgent), api/setup.py and the CLI with --claude/--gemini flags and ~12 agent-name branches, launchers.py, harness.py (Claude-only onboarding), skills.py dirs, sessions.py (Claude env vars only). Today only Claude gets session-start context, only Claude and Gemini get prompt capture, only Claude gets pre-compact and commands; no agent gets stop/session-end. A new agent costs 6-8 files when hooks are involved. Command hooks with JSON on stdin are converging: Gemini CLI (SessionStart, SessionEnd, BeforeAgent, PreCompress... in settings.json), Codex (hooks.json in .codex/: SessionStart with source incl. compact, UserPromptSubmit, Stop; additionalContext), Copilot CLI (sessionStart, sessionEnd, userPromptSubmitted, preToolUse, postToolUse; PascalCase names accepted so Claude-format configs work); opencode/Kilo are plugin-based; Aider has neither MCP nor hooks. So a descriptor per agent plus a few shared hook-config styles, normalizers and emitters, with a fallback ladder (native hook > plugin > MCP first-call > MCP instructions > instruction text), makes a new agent mostly data.

data.question: How can ddflow support the same features, hooks, prompts and onboarding on every coding agent, with a minimal surface for adding a new one?

data.body: Operator 2026-10-05: hooks, prompts, onboarding and features must work on all supported agents (Claude, Copilot, Codex, Gemini, opencode, Kilo, Qwen Code, Aider, Windsurf, Antigravity, Cursor, Cline/Roo, Goose, Amp, ...), and adding one later must not mean rewriting code. chunk_findings.detail: `missing = tmp_path / "not-a-repo"` is never created (no `mkdir()`/`write_text()`), so the path does not exist at the time `D.staged_diff(missing)` and `D.stale_mentions(missing, DOC_GLOBS, [])` are called. The test's whole point is to "make git actually fail" and observe `returncode != 0 -> None`; but `services/docsync.py`'s git invocations (like the test helpers `_git`/`_commit`) pass the repo as the subprocess working directory. With a `cwd=` invocation, `subprocess.run(["git", ...], cwd=<nonexistent>)` raises `FileNotFoundError` in the parent before git is ever executed, so the test errors out on the *unmutated* code instead of exercising the returncode branch — contradicting the block comment's claim that "every one ... passes on the real code". The directory name (`not-a-repo`) shows the intent was a directory that exists but is not a git repo (which yields git exit 128 → `None`); that requires `missing.mkdir()` (or using `tmp_path` directly). Only if `staged_diff` happens to invoke git via `-C <path>` rather than `cwd=<path>` does the current form avoid the exception, in which case the test would work but would not be testing the intended "git exits non-zero" environment reliably.

data.how: For each finding, run the exact counterexample it names against the current tree. It reproduces -> fix, with the reproduction as the regression test. It does not -> record 'refuted' with that command as the probe, and move on.
data.rule: Treat every finding from a reviewer (gate, critic, rubber_duck) as a claim to be reproduced, never as a fact. Reproduce it; when it does not reproduce, record it refuted with the probe that shows it false. Do not change code or tests on a finding you have not reproduced, and do not reopen a passed gate because a second pass contradicted itself.
data.summary: On B-docsync-mutants the only cross-family reviewer (Qwen, config-disabled for off-contract output) first returned no counterexample, then on a later pass returned two findings that inverted its own first pass (claiming two tests pass on their mutant); the per-mutant runs showed both were false. A reviewer's output is a hypothesis: reproduce it before it changes anything, and record the refutation when it does not hold.
data.title: A reviewer's finding is not evidence until it is reproduced; refute it against the probe before acting
data.why: A model that is off contract, or rewarded for finding things, produces confident false findings. The gate prompt already says an uncertain reviewer must report nothing; that only holds if downstream agents verify before acting. Acting on an unreproduced finding either damages correct code or forces a pointless re-review cycle.

data.text: MCP tool calls here time out before long commands finish. Run long test/gate commands detached with `ddflow job run <item> '<cmd>'` and read the log it returns, or run command gates through the `ddflow` CLI in bash.

Cross-family review was the friction. lan-deepseek (the roborev/critic reviewer) is the SAME family as this author (deepseek), so it cannot satisfy reviewer independence; the only cross-family model, Qwen at 127.0.0.1:8000, is config-disabled (gates=[]) because it stalls. Running it by hand: with thinking on it hit the token cap reasoning; with thinking off it answered but drifted past its verdict, and a second pass produced two findings that inverted its first pass and were provably false (the per-mutant runs killed both). Recorded rubber_duck/critic with model=Qwen and NO reviewed_sha, so ddflow used the reviewer I actually ran rather than roborev's same-family record. Also: the MCP client times out before any long call (a one-file pytest run is ~90s), so every test/review run went through `ddflow job run`.

chunk_findings.detail: The extraction regex requires the layer name and the module name to be *contiguous* across the slash: `\b(core|infra|services|api|views|surfaces)/([A-Za-z_]\w*)\.py\b`. But the document's primary module listing — the layer map code block, which is exactly where the reported bug lived (`services/ queue, ... health, setup`) — lists modules *after whitespace*, e.g. `services/   gates.py, leases.py,` and `api/        lifecycle.py, items.py,`. With three-plus spaces between `services/` and `gates.py`, the regex matches nothing on any layer-map line. Only the inline table cells (`| services/leases.py |`, `| api/lifecycle.py |`) are validated. Demonstration: edit the map line to `services/   queue.py, gates.py, ...` reintroducing the original stale name `queue.py` (which does not exist), and `test_every_module_named_in_the_architecture_doc_exists` still passes — `named` never contains `services/queue.py`, so the test that exists specifically to catch this drift does not guard the block the drift occurred in. The docstring's claim that it "walks every `layer/name.py` reference in the document" is therefore false for the layer map, leaving the layer-map column (including any map-only entry such as `services/importer.py`, `api/items.py`, `api/knowledge.py`, `views/human.py`) unverified.

data.how: In a fake server, decrement the in-flight counter right after simulating the work (the delay), before send_response/wfile.write, with a one-shot flag so the finally is only a safety net. peak is then deterministic (1 sequential, N concurrent). Prefer this to a timing ratio (t_par < t_seq/2), which distorts under load.
data.rule: Release a request counter when the work it represents ends, BEFORE writing the response; assert concurrency by that mechanism (the count during the work), never by a wall-clock ratio. A counter kept until after wfile.write/response-send is descheduled under load, so a strictly sequential client reads its count as 2.
data.title: A test double that counts a request in flight until AFTER it writes the response measures the socket, not the work
data.why: fix-B32e97ebbb8: _Fake released in_flight in a finally AFTER wfile.write; a client starts the next sequential chunk the instant it reads the previous response, so when the server thread was descheduled the next request overlapped the not-yet-decremented one and a max_concurrency=1 run read peak==2 -- the concurrency test then flaked only under the end-to-end scenario load. Reproduced 1/40 sequential runs under load before, 0/40 after.

chunk_findings.detail:
The status dispatch is not exhaustive:

```python
if status == G.REGRESSION_COULD_NOT_RUN:      return "could-not-run", ev
if status == G.REGRESSION_PASSES_ON_PREFIX:   return "passed-on-prefix", ev
if status == G.REGRESSION_FAILS_ON_FIX:       return "failed-on-fix", ev
return "verified", ev
```

Every value of `status` that is not one of those three constants is reported as `"verified"`. The three named constants are all *refusal* / *could-not-run* outcomes; the only reason the fall-through is ever correct is that `verify_regression_test` happens to have exactly one success status and no other terminal statuses. If it returns any additional status — an internal/git/setup error distinct from `REGRESSION_COULD_NOT_RUN`, a `not-applicable`/skipped status, or a status added later — a bug whose regression test was never actually shown to fail on the pre-fix tree and pass on the fixed tree is recorded as `"verified"`, with `ev` as its evidence. That is exactly the "false verified" the feature is supposed to make impossible ("record could-not-run (never verified)").

Concrete demonstration: call `_verify_regression(repo, cfg, st, bug_id, ["tests/test_bug.py::test_regression"], verify_regression=True, reason="")` in an environment where `gates.verify_regression_test(...)` resolves its prefix tree but returns, say, `G.REGRESSION_ERROR` (or any constant other than the three checked). The test is never confirmed to fail-first, yet the function returns `("verified", ev)`, and the bug's fix is accepted as verified.

The safe shape is to check the one expected success status explicitly (`if status == G.REGRESSION_VERIFIED: return "verified", ev`) and map any unrecognized status to `"could-not-run"` (recorded) rather than success.

chunk_findings.detail: `command` is computed once, with the fixed tree as its root: `TS.run_command(defn.command, tests, tree)`. The only reason to hand `run_command` a tree is to resolve the selected test selection (node-id paths / rootdir / runner) against that tree, so the resulting string is bound to `tree`. The pre-fix run then replays that same string — `run = GateDef(..., command=command)`; `run_command_gate(run, ptree)` — against a *different* worktree. Wherever `run_command` emitted a tree-rooted path (e.g. it renders `pytest` as `pytest <tree>/tests/test_x.py::test_y`, or pins `--rootdir <tree>`), the "pre-fix" invocation still collects and imports the fixed source. Demo: a regression test that genuinely fails on base; `run_command` returns `pytest /abs/worktree-fixed/tests/test_x.py::test_y`; `run_command_gate(run, ptree)` runs that absolute command, so the test passes, `pre_outcome == "passed"`, and the function returns `passed-on-prefix`, refusing a test that does fail against the unfixed code. The pre-fix invocation must rebuild the command for `ptree` (e.g. `TS.run_command(defn.command, tests, ptree)`) rather than reusing the fixed tree's command.

chunk_findings.detail: The new test module never exercises the “fails on the fixed tree” refusal that the feature docstring and task intent promise. Every test uses either `FAILS_FIRST` (which passes on the fixed tree) or `ALWAYS_PASSES` (which passes on both trees); no test supplies a regression test that fails on the fixed tree. Given a test id that fails on both the pre-fix and fixed trees—e.g. `def test_f(): assert f() == 99`—an implementation that only checks `prefix_outcome == "failed"` and ignores `fix_outcome` would still record `regression_verified == "verified"` and close the bug. The suite has no case to catch that false verification, so the change does not verify the “fails on the fixed one” half of its stated contract.

Existing kinds become built-in doc types with one generated section. Loader: stdlib tomllib only; resolution order and `extends` merge (sections merged by id, a child may drop one with `remove = true`); unknown keys refused with file:line; every error names the file. data.body: A source yields plain data for a section, rendered through the existing sandboxed Jinja2 environment (registry.py:320) with the section's template (inline or file). Sources: kind:<name>[.<key>] reuses an existing DocKind.data(); query: a declarative, safe record query over State -- kind (task|phase|bug|decision|lesson|research|session|memory|rule|item), state, tags, phase, since, owner, sort, limit, fields -- no expressions, no code, validated at load (this is what lets a user build TODO.md = open tasks tagged todo + open bugs, without Python); fragments:<name> aggregates doc.fragment_added entries (towncrier/changesets style: parallel agents never edit the same lines); file:<path>[#anchor] includes a tracked file or one heading's section (path-safe, inside the repo, size-capped); cmd: runs a command declared in operator config with a timeout and no shell, output size-capped and redacted, `unavailable` (never empty-and-passed) when the binary is missing; ask/draft/static are placeholders handled by ownership. The 8 shipped kinds are re-expressed as shipped doctype files whose single generated section has source kind:<name>; golden tests prove byte-identical export output and that [export.<doc>] config keeps working unchanged.

data.body: Event kinds with first writers (strict fold): doc.type_added/doc.type_changed/doc.type_removed (an agent's add is surfaced in brief and doctor until acked; the operator may lock), doc.created (type, path, template digest), doc.answered (doc, section, text, answered_by operator|agent, source prompt), doc.fragment_added (doc, fragment set, text, item), doc.draft_proposed / doc.draft_accepted / doc.draft_rejected (by, model, family, reason), doc.checked (report digest, findings counts), doc.retired. Fold to State.docs[path] = type, sections answered, drafts pending, last check, last refresh, owner. Free text is redacted and fenced as data with provenance (B-security-provenance). Replay rebuilds a document's ddflow-owned and answered content from the log. Tests per handler, unknown kind still refused, replay determinism.
data.title: Documents as first-class records: doc.* events (type added/changed/removed, created, answered, fragment added, draft proposed/accepted/rejected, checked, retired), folded into State.docs, replayable

data.body: Map each section to a named region of the one marker grammar (B-tpl-regions), carrying owner= and status= attributes. generated: spliced on refresh, a hand edit refused/merged/moved per B-tpl-merge. human: written only at creation (skeleton text or the operator's interview answer), never again; ddflow only validates it. seeded: the stored base render (digest + body in the log) lets a later template version be applied as a 3-way merge (git merge-file) -- copier's update model -- conflicts shown, never overwritten. draft: written with status=draft author=<model>; turns into human or seeded on doc.draft_accepted. Missing required human content is a visible `<!-- ddflow:ask <doc>/<section> "question" -->` placeholder, never invented text. Creating a collection member allocates {seq} without clashes across clones (same rule as B-id-decide). Tests: each mode across create, refresh, hand edit, template upgrade.
data.title: Section ownership on the region engine: generated (re-rendered, hash-guarded), human (never written after creation, only validated), seeded (written once, template upgrades by 3-way merge), draft (marked until accepted); creation from the skeleton with ask placeholders

data.body: `ddflow doc new <type> [<name>]` creates the document from its skeleton and asks each ask-section's prompt on a TTY (typed answers, defaults, regex/length validators, `when` conditions on earlier answers); `ddflow doc pending` lists unanswered questions across documents; `ddflow doc answer <doc>/<section> --text|stdin` records doc.answered and writes the section. Over MCP the tool returns the pending questions with the instruction to ask the operator verbatim; an answer recorded by an agent must carry answered_by=operator plus the operator's words (session prompt id) or it is refused unless filed as a draft. The brief gains a budgeted line 'N document sections wait on you'. Prompt template /doc (overridable via .ddflow/prompts). Tests: TTY interview with a fake stdin, condition skipping, agent self-answer refused, replay restores answers.
data.title: Content from the user: ddflow doc new runs a copier-style interview over ask sections (question, default, validator, condition); over MCP the agent relays the questions verbatim and records the operator's answers; the agent cannot answer a human section itself

data.body: `ddflow doc draft <doc>/<section> --text|stdin` (agent) writes the draft region status=draft author=<model> and records doc.draft_proposed; `doc accept|reject <doc>/<section> [--reason]` records the outcome (accept by a person by default; [docs].draft_acceptance = operator|cross_family lets a reviewer of another model family accept, the same independence rule as code review). `doc show --drafts` prints pending drafts with a diff against the current text. Validation reports an unaccepted draft as a finding (warn/block by severity), never as content. Tests: propose/accept/reject, same-family acceptance refused when cross_family, a rejected draft leaves the placeholder.
data.title: Drafted prose with approval: an agent may propose text for a human or draft section; it is marked as an unaccepted draft until the operator (or, if configured, a different-family reviewer) accepts it; an unaccepted draft fails validation in block mode

data.body: Stdlib-only structural parser of Markdown headings, sections, code fences, tables, lists, links and YAML front matter (a safe subset; no dependency). Checks (mdschema-style, from the type's TOML): required sections present and in order; heading literal/regex, level, no skipped levels, unique headings; per section: required_text / forbidden_text regexes, min/max words, code_blocks {lang, min}, has_table, has_list, links resolve (reuse docscheck's local link/anchor checker), no unanswered ask placeholder, no unaccepted draft, dates not expired (`review_by`); front matter checked against a JSON-Schema subset (type, required, enum, pattern). Rubrics: scored checks a type can name (shipped: security-policy after OpenSSF Scorecard -- contact, disclosure terms, response time; keep-a-changelog; madr). An external linter per type ([docs.types.<t>].lint_command, e.g. vale or markdownlint) runs as a configured command and is `unavailable` when absent. Findings plug into `ddflow docs check` and its digest (B-docs-gate-evidence) with the [docs].severity default warn. Tests per rule, golden report.
data.title: Validate a document against its type: required sections in order, heading rules, per-section content rules (required/forbidden text, word bounds, code blocks, tables, links, no open ask placeholder), front matter schema, scored rubrics; a check family of ddflow docs check

data.body: Today rules.matches_globs (services/rules.py:167) has no caller, so a rule cannot be attached to a document. Wire it: claim and brief include the rules (budgeted, ranked) whose globs overlap the item's globs -- generic, benefits code too -- and, for a document path, the type's guidance block and section prompts. Users add per-document rules with `ddflow rule add --globs SECURITY.md ...` or in the type's `rules` list (both end up as ddflow rules with provenance). The doc-review gate prompt includes them so a cross-family reviewer checks the prose against them. Tests: a rule on docs/**.md reaches the brief of an item touching docs/a.md and not of one touching src/.
data.title: Rules and guidance per document: a type's guidance (audience, tone, genre, style guide) and every ddflow rule whose globs match a document reach the agent when its item touches that document; wire Rule.globs, which is stored but consulted nowhere today

data.body: Triggers declared per type ([doctype.triggers]): depends_on globs -- an item whose diff touches them gets a 'doc due' obligation for that document listed in gate_status (Swimm-style coupling); on = [version.cut, bug.fixed:security, decision.recorded, phase.completed, research.confirmed, ...] create a due record; stale_after = '180d' and schedule register with the cadence/P-schedule machinery (docs-correctness job); manual = `ddflow doc refresh`. An obligation is satisfied by the docs gate evidence containing that document's check digest for the current tree, or by `gate skip` with a reason -- never by silence. Migrate [enforce].readme_with_code/readme_code_globs/readme_files into the shipped README type's depends_on with identical defaults and behaviour (the old keys keep working, doctor suggests the move). Tests: each trigger, satisfaction, the readme migration is behaviour-identical.
data.title: When a document is due: depends_on code globs (code-to-doc coupling for every type, generalising readme_with_code), log-event triggers (version cut, security bug fixed, decision recorded, phase close, research confirmed), schedule and stale_after, manual; a due document is a visible obligation the docs gate must answer

data.body: A task with doc=<type>[:<name>] gets globs = the document target(s) automatically and the [workflow.pipeline.doc] pipeline (default from D-doc-types: outline -> user_content (passes when no required ask is pending) -> draft -> doc_check (mechanical, B-dt-validate) -> doc_review (agent gate, reviewer of another model family, with the type's rules) -> merge); editable with `ddflow workflow pipeline --kind doc` and over MCP; code gates that do not apply are absent from this pipeline rather than skipped. The phase-level docs gate extends B-rm-workflow's refresh from ROADMAP to every selected or due document: refresh generated sections, run validation, attach digests. data.body: Ask the operator and record D-doc-search: (1) scope: [docs].check_paths + [enforce].doc_globs + every doc-type target, minus doc_exclude and generated views (opt-in) -- recommended; (2) index in .ddflow/local/docs.db (git-ignored, derived from files, rebuildable, never committed), separate from the log index -- recommended; (3) backends: FTS5 porter + FTS5 trigram for typo tolerance, fused by reciprocal rank, LIKE fallback; embeddings optional as a companion (local command or MCP) off by default; (4) watcher: auto (MCP server thread + opportunistic scans + git hooks), poll, or off; (5) budgets: debounce 1.5 s, batch 50 files, 200 ms CPU per tick, queue cap; (6) RAG payload: snippets with path:lines and heading path, fenced as data, default 1500 tokens, never whole files unless asked.
data.title: Operator decisions for documentation search: scope, index location, fuzzy and semantic backends, watcher default, throttling budgets, what an agent's RAG reply may contain

data.body: Pure, stdlib. A chunk = (path, chunk_id = path#anchor~ordinal, heading_path ['Install','From source'], line_start, line_end, text, sha256, kind prose|code|table, region doc/section + ownership when inside ddflow markers). Splits on headings, then on paragraphs past max_chars with overlap; never inside a code fence; front matter becomes metadata. Anchors computed as GitHub does (reuse docscheck's slug rules). Deterministic: same file -> same chunks and ids; an edit changes only the touched chunks' hashes. Tests on tricky files: setext headings, nested fences, very long sections, CRLF, non-UTF-8 (skipped and reported).
data.title: Heading-aware document chunker: Markdown, reStructuredText, AsciiDoc and text into sections with heading path, line range, stable chunk id, content hash, code-fence awareness, size cap with overlap, ddflow region and doc-type tags

data.body: Tables: files(path, size, mtime_ns, inode, sha256, doctype, indexed_at), chunks(...), chunks_fts (porter unicode61), chunks_tri (trigram, when the sqlite build supports it; else fuzzy degrades to the textsim path and says so). Scope resolver (scope.py): tracked files only (git ls-files), matching the decided globs, size and binary caps. Upsert per file by sha256 (unchanged content is not rechunked); delete rows for vanished files; schema bump forces rebuild. Secrets redacted before text enters the index (export/safe.redact_text) so a search cannot surface one. A single writer under a lock file with timeouts; readers never block on the writer (WAL). Tests: incremental update touches only changed rows, rename, delete, schema bump, no-FTS5 fallback, a secret is not findable.
data.title: Documentation index: a separate derived sqlite (.ddflow/local/docs.db) of files and chunks with FTS5 porter and trigram tables, incremental upsert by content hash, deletions, schema version, lock and atomic swap, LIKE fallback, redaction before indexing

data.body: Query pipeline: normalise (code-aware split from core/textsim), BM25 over chunks_fts, trigram matches over chunks_tri for misspellings ('confgure' finds 'configure'), reciprocal-rank fusion, boosts for heading-path and document-title hits, optional textsim cosine rerank of the top 50, dedupe adjacent chunks of one section. Modes: ranked (default), --fuzzy-off, --exact, --regex (reusing search.check_regex safety). Filters: --path glob, --type, --section, --limit. `ddflow search` gains source `doc` (on by default) and recall shows top doc hits labelled DOC within its budget. Precision measured on a labelled query set from this repository's docs (recorded as research), with a regression test on that set.
data.title: Ranked and fuzzy documentation search: BM25 + trigram typo tolerance fused by reciprocal rank, heading and title boosts, filters (path glob, doc type, section), exact and regex modes; ddflow docs search and a doc source in ddflow search and recall

data.body: Queue file .ddflow/local/docindex.queue (append-only lines path+reason+ts, compacted; dedup by path, latest wins). Worker: takes the lock non-blocking (another worker running -> return), waits for a quiet debounce window, processes at most batch_max_files and max_cpu_ms_per_tick per tick, sleeps/yields between ticks, stops early when a foreground request arrives (a flag file / in-process event), lowers its priority where the OS allows (os.nice). Idempotent by sha256, so a crash mid-batch just repeats work. Backpressure: past queue_cap, collapse to a 'rescan scope' marker instead of growing. Status: queue length, oldest age, last error. Config [docsearch] debounce_ms, batch_max_files, max_cpu_ms_per_tick, queue_cap. Tests with a fake clock: coalescing, debounce, budget respected, crash recovery, yield.
data.title: Throttled index update queue: a persisted, coalescing queue of changed doc paths drained by one locked worker under debounce, batch and CPU budgets, yielding to foreground calls; crash-safe and idempotent

data.body: Three detectors, all enqueue only (never index inline except as below): (a) stat scan of the scope (size, mtime_ns, inode vs files table) throttled to once per scan_interval_s, run at brief, next, claim, search and MCP tool calls; (b) git hooks installed by setup/hooks (opt-in like other hooks) enqueue the paths a commit/merge/checkout changed (git diff --name-only); (c) in the MCP server, a daemon thread: watchfiles if importable (optional, no hard dependency), else polling with exponential backoff when idle; it survives exceptions (logged, restarted with backoff) and never blocks the request loop. A search reads the index as is: when the queue holds paths in its scope the reply says 'index N files behind', and a queried file under small_file_bytes is indexed inline first. [docsearch].watch = auto|poll|off. Tests: each detector with a temp repo, the thread dies and is restarted, a request is not delayed past budget while a large batch drains.
data.title: Monitor documentation files for changes: cheap stat scans at opportunistic points, git hooks (post-commit, post-merge, post-checkout, post-rewrite) and a watcher thread in the long-running MCP server (inotify/FSEvents via watchfiles when installed, polling with backoff otherwise) feed the queue

data.body: Hits = path:line_start-line_end, heading path, score, snippet cut around the matched terms (redacted text), chunk id. `docs read <chunk_id|path#anchor> [--around N]` returns exactly that section (plus N neighbours), so the agent pays for one section instead of a file. `docs ask "question" [--budget TOKENS]` = top-k chunks across files, merged where adjacent, deduplicated by textsim, ordered by score, truncated to the budget, each with a citation, wrapped as data (provenance fence) -- the agent's model writes the answer; ddflow adds no LLM by default (an optional local summariser is a companion, off). MCP resource template ddflow://docs/{path}#{anchor}. MCP instructions and the brief tell the agent to search docs before reading whole documentation files. Each pack records bytes served vs whole-file bytes so `ddflow docs search --stats` reports tokens saved. Tests: budget never exceeded, citations exact, read-by-anchor matches the file.
data.title: Token-saving retrieval for agents: ddflow_docs_search returns budgeted, cited, fenced snippets; ddflow_docs_read expands a chunk or path#heading with neighbours; ddflow docs ask builds a deduplicated context pack within a token budget; an MCP resource per document section; nudges to search before reading files

data.body: [docsearch].semantic = off|companion; the companion contract: stdin JSON lines of texts -> stdout vectors (any local model: ollama, llama.cpp, sentence-transformers wrapper), with a timeout. Vectors in docs.db (float32 blobs); cosine in pure Python over the BM25/trigram candidate set, or sqlite-vec if loadable. A model change invalidates all vectors (model id recorded). Embedding runs inside the queue worker's budget. Listed in `ddflow companions` with what it buys and what it would run; never installed without asking. Hybrid fusion weight configurable. Tests with a fake embedder: only changed chunks re-embedded, model change rebuilds, absent companion -> lexical results plus an explicit 'semantic unavailable' note.

chunk_findings.detail:
The status dispatch is not exhaustive:

```python
if status == G.REGRESSION_COULD_NOT_RUN:      return "could-not-run", ev
if status == G.REGRESSION_PASSES_ON_PREFIX:   return "passed-on-prefix", ev
if status == G.REGRESSION_FAILS_ON_FIX:       return "failed-on-fix", ev
return "verified", ev
```

Every value of `status` that is not one of those three constants is reported as `"verified"`. The three named constants are all *refusal* / *could-not-run* outcomes; the only reason the fall-through is ever correct is that `verify_regression_test` happens to have exactly one success status and no other terminal statuses. If it returns any additional status — an internal/git/setup error distinct from `REGRESSION_COULD_NOT_RUN`, a `not-applicable`/skipped status, or a status added later — a bug whose regression test was never actually shown to fail on the pre-fix tree and pass on the fixed tree is recorded as `"verified"`, with `ev` as its evidence. That is exactly the "false verified" the feature is supposed to make impossible ("record could-not-run (never verified)").

Concrete demonstration: call `_verify_regression(repo, cfg, st, bug_id, ["tests/test_bug.py::test_regression"], verify_regression=True, reason="")` in an environment where `gates.verify_regression_test(...)` resolves its prefix tree but returns, say, `G.REGRESSION_ERROR` (or any constant other than the three checked). The test is never confirmed to fail-first, yet the function returns `("verified", ev)`, and the bug's fix is accepted as verified.

The safe shape is to check the one expected success status explicitly (`if status == G.REGRESSION_VERIFIED: return "verified", ev`) and map any unrecognized status to `"could-not-run"` (recorded) rather than success.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge.py:1185 (`_verify_regression`, the final `return "verified", ev`)

chunk_findings.detail: `command` is computed once, with the fixed tree as its root: `TS.run_command(defn.command, tests, tree)`. The only reason to hand `run_command` a tree is to resolve the selected test selection (node-id paths / rootdir / runner) against that tree, so the resulting string is bound to `tree`. The pre-fix run then replays that same string — `run = GateDef(..., command=command)`; `run_command_gate(run, ptree)` — against a *different* worktree. Wherever `run_command` emitted a tree-rooted path (e.g. it renders `pytest` as `pytest <tree>/tests/test_x.py::test_y`, or pins `--rootdir <tree>`), the "pre-fix" invocation still collects and imports the fixed source. Demo: a regression test that genuinely fails on base; `run_command` returns `pytest /abs/worktree-fixed/tests/test_x.py::test_y`; `run_command_gate(run, ptree)` runs that absolute command, so the test passes, `pre_outcome == "passed"`, and the function returns `passed-on-prefix`, refusing a test that does fail against the unfixed code. The pre-fix invocation must rebuild the command for `ptree` (e.g. `TS.run_command(defn.command, tests, ptree)`) rather than reusing the fixed tree's command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates.py::verify_regression_test (pre-fix run reuses the fixed-tree command)

chunk_findings.detail: The new test module never exercises the “fails on the fixed tree” refusal that the feature docstring and task intent promise. Every test uses either `FAILS_FIRST` (which passes on the fixed tree) or `ALWAYS_PASSES` (which passes on both trees); no test supplies a regression test that fails on the fixed tree. Given a test id that fails on both the pre-fix and fixed trees—e.g. `def test_f(): assert f() == 99`—an implementation that only checks `prefix_outcome == "failed"` and ignores `fix_outcome` would still record `regression_verified == "verified"` and close the bug. The suite has no case to catch that false verification, so the change does not verify the “fails on the fixed one” half of its stated contract.

data.claim: Little copy-paste (pylint: 5 clusters >=6 lines) but the same concern is solved many ways, and the variants carry bugs others fixed. Measured on main e4342e62 (73.4k lines, 176 modules): each command declared 3x (cli.build_parser one 1,229-line function with 131 subparsers/414 arguments; mcp.TOOLS ~2,670 lines, 107 tools; commands/* ~4,400; 33 of 51 CLI body tuples equal an MCP payload; parity test with 6 exemption tables; README says 92 tools, actual 107); 6 rankers and 4 tokenizers (store BM25 + LIKE fallback, textsim TF-IDF, skills hand BM25, rules Jaccard, rules regex/substring) and 7 slug helpers; git via W.git plus 6 private wrappers and 22 raw calls, 7 git calls without timeout, 7 shell runners of which 5 do not kill the process group (confirmed: orphaned child, bug Bed0f5b6d99); 4 atomic writers, 33 plain write_text of files that matter (MCP configs, hooks, DDFLOW.md), 2 flocks (one never times out), 9 copies of the self-ignoring dir, 4 TOML emitters (confirmed quoting bug B28cab0652a), 29 repo-relative path sites with 5 behaviours, 5 managed-region implementations, 25 hashing sites; 'gate settled' defined 4 ways, ~200 outcome string literals, 6 ad-hoc DAG walks; 167 knobs each declared twice, 21 enum knobs unchecked (confirmed B-eea0744a7b); 9 text clippers, 2 redaction engines; 104 functions grade D+ (mcp.Server.handle CC 59); services return 3 result shapes; layer violations (core->config 5, services<->views, surfaces->services/infra 59) and 570 deferred imports. Planned work would multiply this: ~12 hand-written CRUD surfaces, ~8 new verb tools, ~9 shipped->project->config loaders, ~6 marker writers, ~8 definition-record families with their own revise/supersede, 5 trigger evaluators, 6 cadence definitions, 4-5 opportunistic tick mechanisms, 3 concurrency limiters, 2 embedding backends, 6 budgeted context injectors, ~10 command runners, 6 approve-by-digest flows; hot files with no split task: api/reporting.py (26 planned edits), services/gates.py (22), api/knowledge.py (22).
data.falsifier: After the phase, a new record family, CLI+MCP command, config knob, shipped asset loader, opportunistic tick, trigger or search source is added by declaring data in one place, with no new argparse/schema/loader/queue/runner code; ratchets show zero raw git/subprocess/write_text/tempfile call sites outside infra.
data.mechanism: Library survey (PyPI JSON, uv pip compile, 2026-10): keep core = Jinja2; tomlkit (MIT, pure, 0 deps) is the one candidate worth vendoring for comment-preserving config writes; optional extras with stdlib fallbacks and a doctor probe: search=rapidfuzz, watch=watchfiles (polling must exist anyway for containers), rag=model2vec+sqlite-vec (no runtime downloads), mcp-sdk only if HTTP transport is wanted (mcp 2.3 pulls 28 packages; FastMCP 68); stdlib graphlib for DAG (networkx needs Python>=3.12 -> test oracle only); FTS5 trigram (SQLite>=3.34, probed) covers fuzzy; git merge-file for 3-way (merge3 is GPL); stdlib atomic write/lock (atomicwrites archived); subprocess git (GitPython/pygit2/dulwich worse for worktrees); dev-only hypothesis, syrupy, import-linter, mutmut. Protocol risk dominates library risk: MCP 2026-07-28 removes initialize, adds server/discover, resultType, ttlMs/cacheScope, deterministic tools/list.
data.probe: radon cc, vulture, pylint duplicate-code over ddflow/ (scratchpad/refac); grep census; four bug probes (orphaned child after shell timeout; Rule.to_toml with a quote; Config.check with typo enums; shared_files with a non-ASCII path); board census of 69 phases / ~281 open tasks.
data.probe_output: All four bugs reproduced and filed (Bed0f5b6d99 high, B28cab0652a, Beea0744a7b, B9c56de9d58).

data.body: Operator 2026-10-05 (verbatim in session s20260929T144138-2948413): research the software and propose a phase for a generic refactoring and unified interfaces for search, file monitoring, processing, CLI, MCP, RAG, indexing, workflow, DAG, optimisation; best libraries; what to refactor and optimise; minimise the code surface; more shared and reusable code with a smaller bug surface; account for planned work. Research R-unify (CONFIRMED; measured on main e4342e62, 73.4k lines). FINDINGS: concerns solved many ways rather than copy-pasted -- commands declared 3x (build_parser 1,229 lines, mcp.TOOLS ~2,670, commands/* ~4,400), 6 rankers/4 tokenizers/7 slug helpers, 6 git wrappers + 22 raw git calls + 7 shell runners (5 leave orphans), 4 atomic writers + 33 plain writes of important files, 4 TOML emitters, 5 region writers, 4 definitions of 'gate settled', 6 DAG walks, 167 knobs declared twice with 21 enums unchecked, 9 clippers, 2 redactors; and ~281 open tasks would add ~12 CRUD surfaces, ~9 asset loaders, ~8 definition-record families, 5 trigger evaluators, 4-5 tick mechanisms, 3 limiters, 2 embedding backends, 6 context injectors, ~10 command runners. Four bugs found and filed (fix-Bed0f5b6d99 orphaned children on timeout, fix-B28cab0652a rule TOML quoting, fix-Beea0744a7b unchecked enum knobs, fix-B9c56de9d58 non-ASCII ls-files) -- fixed first, bugs-first. LIBRARIES (policy for B-uni-decide): core stays Jinja2; vendor tomlkit for comment-preserving config writes; optional extras with stdlib fallbacks and a doctor probe: [search] rapidfuzz, [watch] watchfiles, [rag] model2vec+sqlite-vec, [mcp-sdk] only for HTTP; stdlib graphlib, FTS5 trigram, git merge-file, subprocess git; dev-only hypothesis, syrupy, import-linter, mutmut; avoid pydantic/FastMCP in core, GitPython/pygit2/dulwich, merge3 (GPL), atomicwrites, networkx at runtime. METHOD: strangler -- each interface lands with a ratchet test counting the old call sites, which only goes down; behaviour is pinned first by golden/property tests; no task changes user-visible behaviour except the bug fixes. BUILDS ON (does not duplicate): B-hot-files splits (B-split-mcp-tools, -cli-parser, -config, -model-handlers, -api-lifecycle), B-relpath-helper, B-json-failures, B149 (MCP 2026-07-28), B-coh-coverage, B-id-generator, B-trigger-model/B-sched-model, B-hx-descriptor/B-hx-hook-core, B-tpl-regions, B-view-list-core (done), B-export-core (done). Order: decide -> guards -> {proc, fsio, knobs, outcomes, graph, textkit} -> {search-core, local-worker, overlay, cmd-core, mcp-protocol, splits} -> {context-pack, def-records, cmd-migrate, cmdrunner, approval, plan-pipeline, kind-pipeline} -> {record-surface, triggers} -> repoint (as each lands) -> acceptance.

data.body: Ask the operator; record D-unify (+ D-dependencies). Recommended answers from R-unify: (1) core runtime dependency stays Jinja2 only; tomlkit vendored under ddflow/_vendor with licence and pinned hash (or core if they prefer pip security updates); (2) optional extras, each imported in exactly one adapter module, with a stdlib fallback and a doctor capability line, a missing extra recorded unavailable never silently degraded: search (rapidfuzz), watch (watchfiles), rag (model2vec + sqlite-vec, no runtime model download), mcp-sdk (only if Streamable HTTP is wanted); (3) dev-only: hypothesis, syrupy, import-linter, mutmut, networkx and markdown-it-py as test oracles; (4) avoid list with reasons; (5) names: `ddflow doc` (documents) vs `ddflow docs` (checks/search) -> one group; `rule` vs `rules` -> one; services/jobs.py (process jobs) vs schedule jobs -> rename one; `search` (records) / `recall` (budgeted) / `docs search` -> one search with sources; (6) migration: strangler + ratchet per interface, behaviour pinned by goldens first, no user-visible change except bug fixes; (7) MCP: serve 2025-11-25 and 2026-07-28 from one engine. Write the decision doc.
